title: Work and home
hookLine: keep the people you work for in view

lines: A DRAWING, A DOG, TWO TEXTS.
cards: Two plates on a kitchen table, and one chair still empty. A child has a drawing ready to show someone. A dog sits by the door with its ears up.

A friend has texted twice. None of them are in anyone's calendar, and none of them will send a reminder. Somewhere else, the person they're waiting for is answering one more email, fixing one more small thing.
They just wait. The old question is who all this work is for. Today: Ecclesiastes.

teach.h: NO END OF ALL HIS LABOR.
teach.b: First, a man with no end to his work. The book of Ecclesiastes describes him: alone, no child, no brother, and still no end of all his labor, his eye never satisfied with riches.
The writer notes the one question he never asks, in the King James words: "For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good?" The writer calls it vanity, and a sore travail. Second, the turn.
For some people, the honest answer to that question is a short list of names. The rent paid, the groceries bought, the school shoes, the trip to see a grandmother.
The work was for them all along. But work has a way of quietly swapping places with the people it was meant to serve. The job grows to fill the evening, and the ones it was for get what's left.

teach.h: SO HE GIVETH HIS BELOVED SLEEP.
teach.b: Psalm 127 says it plainly: "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Readers take that line in different ways.
Some hear trust in God, who builds the house. Some hear permission to rest. Either way, the psalm doesn't praise the late night.
Leaving on time is a small act, and it says something.
To the people at home: you are the reason, not the leftover. To the work: you matter, and you are not everything. Some days the work really can't wait, and that's honest too.
But if it never waits, the people do. And people who wait long enough sometimes stop waiting.

how: People who try to keep work and home in balance often set a fixed time to stop, close the laptop or leave the workplace at that hour, and protect certain evenings or meals for the people at home.

o: a psalm about rising early and working late
a book of Paul's letters about church work
the Bible book that asks: for whom do I labor?

games.q: work and home — tap the pairs.

s: Ecclesiastes praises the man whose work never ends
the writer calls his endless labor vanity, and a sore travail.
Psalm 127 says rising early and sitting up late is vain
"it is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late."
the man in Ecclesiastes works for a large family
he is alone, with no child and no brother, and still never stops.

games.q: it's ten to six. you planned to leave on time, and a "quick" request lands. what do you do?
o: stay, as always. it'll only take a minute.
ask who you're working for, and whether it can wait until morning.
leave without reading it at all.
games.why: Ecclesiastes asks who the work is for. some requests truly can't wait. others can, and the people at home are waiting too.

practice: Bring to mind the people your work is for, not the clients or the boss, but a partner, a child, a parent, a friend, even yourself. Picture one of them at the moment you usually arrive late.
Then picture closing the laptop at a set hour and walking in while they're still waiting; if you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Ecclesiastes. Whose Preacher asks the question some never do: for whom do I labor, and deprive myself of good? Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: they're waiting. The work was for them all along. That's day nine hundred twenty-seven.
